analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $10.10 and lifts wages for tipped workers.
analysis.headline: The bill had 40 Senate sponsors and cosponsors and was placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in steps — to $8.20, then $9.15, then $10.10 an hour — and then adjusted it automatically each year with inflation so it would not erode again. It also raises the separate lower minimum wage for tipped workers (now $2.13) up to 70% of the full minimum wage. To soften the cost for businesses, it extends tax rules letting businesses immediately deduct up to $500,000 in equipment purchases and treat restaurant and retail renovation costs as deductible business property.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage, especially in food service, retail, and other low-wage industries, who would see their hourly pay rise in steps to $10.10 and then keep pace with inflation. Tipped workers would benefit most: the bill phases their cash wage up to 70% of the full minimum, replacing the current $2.13 base. The tax extensions benefit businesses that buy equipment or renovate restaurants and stores.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps — $8.20, $9.15, then $10.10 an hour — then adjusts it annually by the Consumer Price Index so future inflation cannot quietly erode it [S2][S3].

Raises the tipped minimum wage from its current floor to $3.00 an hour and then phases it up each year until it equals 70% of the regular minimum wage, directly boosting pay for restaurant servers and other tipped workers [S2][S3].
Requires the Labor Department to publish each upcoming increase 60 days ahead in the Federal Register and online, so employers and workers can plan for it [S2][S3].

Extends the $500,000 business expensing allowance and the treatment of leasehold, restaurant, and retail improvement property as deductible business property through 2016, easing the transition cost for employers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay the minimum wage — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other labor-intensive services — would bear higher payroll costs. The tax extensions would forgo some federal revenue (businesses deduct more of their investment immediately), which the broader public ultimately finances.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers like restaurants and retailers

drawbacks.text: Businesses in low-margin, labor-intensive industries such as food service would face sharply higher payroll costs, and the bill phases the tipped wage up by as much as $0.95 an hour per year toward 70% of the full minimum, a large change for restaurant owners [S3].

The bill pairs the wage increase with an extension of generous business tax expensing through 2016, which reduces federal revenue and gives tax benefits to profitable firms regardless of whether they pay any worker more [S3].

As with any minimum wage increase, some employers would respond to higher labor costs by raising prices, cutting hours, or automating tasks; economists debate how large these effects are, but they are the standard cost an honest supporter must acknowledge (general knowledge of how wage floors work).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct and large: a raise to $10.10 for workers at the bottom of the pay scale, plus automatic inflation indexing — a structural fix, since the federal minimum wage has historically lost value between congressional updates. The costs fall on a smaller set of employers, many of whom also receive offsetting tax benefits under the same bill. The Section 179 extension is a concession that reduces the bill's net revenue benefit, but the wage provisions are the substance, and they outweigh a modest, temporary tax extension. The design is reasonable — phased in over years, with advance notice for employers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and put it on its calendar, and in spring 2014 leadership moved three times to bring it up, but no vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin, joined by Majority Leader Harry Reid, introduced the bill on November 19, 2013 [S5][S3].
39 senators — 38 Democrats and 1 Independent — signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and placed it on the calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 250), a step short of floor debate [S5].

In late March and early April 2014, a motion to proceed to consideration of the bill was made three times on the Senate floor, but the record shows the Senate never reached a vote on the bill itself [S5].
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, with the bill still stalled, and it died without either chamber acting on it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the minimum wage — especially restaurants and retailers that rely on tipped workers — avoided both the higher wage floor and the phased increase in tipped pay. No worker gained anything from the bill's death.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Minimum Wage Fairness Act and made repeated motions to proceed to bring it to the Senate floor in spring 2014.

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Joined Harkin in introducing the bill and made motions on the floor in March and April 2014 to proceed to its consideration.

for.name: 38 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the backing of most of the Senate Democratic caucus.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Senate minority, holding enough seats to block floor debate
against.what_they_did: Denied the bill the supermajority needed to begin floor debate; the Senate's three motions to proceed in spring 2014 never resulted in the bill coming up for a vote, and no vote on the bill occurred before the Congress ended.

against.name: Restaurant and retail trade groups
against.role: Industry lobbying against a higher minimum wage and tipped-wage increase
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill publicly during the 2014 debate over the federal minimum wage.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent, and the bill never attracted the Republican support it needed to overcome the Senate's 60-vote threshold to begin debate.

industries.note: The bill would raise their payroll costs substantially, including a tipped minimum that phases up to 70% of the full wage — but that same increase is what puts money directly in servers' and kitchen workers' paychecks. The bill partially offsets their costs by extending tax expensing for restaurant improvement property [S3].

Higher minimum wages raise labor costs for large and small retailers alike, but the bill extends the $500,000 Section 179 expensing allowance and retail improvement property treatment through 2016, giving retailers a meaningful tax benefit in the same legislation [S2][S3].
Workers at or near the federal minimum — disproportionately in food service and retail — would gain the entire value of the increase, which is the point of the bill [S2].
